text: Chapters one and two covered distributed systems in the abstract: availability, consistency, messaging, failure handling. This chapter starts applying them, beginning with a platform many of you already work in. Salesforce's multi-tenant cloud is itself a distributed system, and some of its most distinctive features exist specifically to enforce ideas you've already learned.

Salesforce runs huge numbers of customer orgs on shared infrastructure. One org running a massive, inefficient query could, in principle, degrade things for every other org sharing that infrastructure. That's the exact same "noisy neighbor" problem any multi-tenant distributed system faces, and it gets solved the same way: hard limits, enforced on every tenant, consistently.

Governor limits cap things like SOQL queries, CPU time, DML statements, and callouts per transaction. That's rate limiting, exactly as this course has described it — a deliberate cap, enforced regardless of what the requester needs, to protect the shared system. Instead of letting one runaway transaction cascade into everyone else's problem, Salesforce fails that one transaction fast. This course won't quote specific limit numbers, since they change between releases — the concept is what matters.

Salesforce also gives you several ways to move work off the synchronous path. Future methods and Queueable Apex hand work off to run later. Batch Apex processes huge volumes in asynchronous chunks. And Platform Events implement publish-subscribe natively — one event, published once, consumed independently by however many subscribers are listening — the same decoupling a message broker gives you anywhere else.

None of this is Salesforce-specific machinery — it's the same handful of ideas from chapters one and two, in Salesforce's own vocabulary. Next, lesson thirteen: designing for failure as a deliberate philosophy, independent of any one platform.
